screens.title: Red Teaming and Adversary Emulation
screens.subtitle: Simulating determined adversaries to test people, processes, and technology

narration.text: In this lesson we move from vulnerability hunting to realistic adversary simulation. Red teaming is a strategic exercise that imitates a determined attacker with objectives, not a checklist. You'll learn how red teams choose goals, operate with limited prior knowledge, and chain tactics, techniques, and procedures to measure an organisation's true resilience. We'll also introduce MITRE ATT&CK as the common language that frames adversary behaviour, and explain how Command and Control frameworks let red teams emulate persistent campaigns while protecting their operations through OPSEC. Finally, you will see how purple teaming turns that adversary insight into stronger detections and response. A concrete example you will revisit is an insider exfiltration scenario mapped to ATT&CK steps, showing the full flow from initial access to exfiltration. Keep in mind a common misconception: red teaming is not merely a louder penetration test; it is goal-focused and designed to test real detection and response. By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the purpose of red teams, identify ATT&CK tactics used in realistic chains, and explain why OPSEC and collaboration with blue teams produce measurable defensive improvements.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Red teaming simulates goal-oriented adversaries using ATT&CK and C2 frameworks while applying OPSEC; results feed purple teaming to improve detection and response.

Orientation

Why it matters

A successful red team exercise reveals gaps that scans miss — social engineering failures, detection blind spots, and process weaknesses that allow adversaries to persist.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives shape practical, measurable skills you will practice during the chapter. First, you will be able to distinguish penetration testing from red teaming by articulating the goal-oriented and black-box nature of red-team operations and why that matters to defenders. Second, you will learn to use the MITRE ATT&CK framework to plan emulations and map detections, which gives you a common language to describe TTPs. Third, you will recognise common C2 frameworks and how they enable persistent control over compromised hosts during an emulation. Finally, you will apply OPSEC principles so red team infrastructure and tradecraft do not compromise the realism of the test, and you will understand how purple teaming turns red findings into defensive improvements. Each objective pairs a skill with its practical relevance: for example, mapping an attack chain to ATT&CK gives defenders targeted detections they can implement immediately. Keep these objectives in mind as practical outcomes, not abstract topics.

screens.title: Penetration Testing vs Red Teaming
screens.subtitle: Scope-led vulnerability assessment contrasted with goal-oriented adversary simulation

narration.text: Start with a clear distinction: penetration testing focuses on identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities within a defined scope, often with white-box or grey-box knowledge. Its primary value is to find technical weaknesses and provide remediation steps. Red teaming shifts the frame. It simulates a determined adversary whose objective is a business-level outcome, such as gaining domain administrator privileges or exfiltrating customer data. Red teams operate with minimal prior knowledge to mimic external attackers and they chain techniques across social engineering, physical access, and technical exploitation. For example, a penetration test might scan a subnet and exploit an exposed service; a red team, given the objective to obtain sensitive data, may use spearphishing to gain initial access, then move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data, measuring whether defenders detect each phase. A frequent misconception is that red teams only need more time—actually, they require a different planning approach, stronger OPSEC, and an emphasis on outcome measurement. As a takeaway, remember that penetration testing answers 'what is vulnerable', while red teaming answers 'how would an adversary achieve this objective', and that difference changes tool choice, rules of engagement, and reporting style. How would you reframe a report to emphasize resilience rather than a list of CVEs?

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: Pen tests find technical flaws; red teams simulate adversaries to validate whether the organisation can detect, respond, and contain goal-driven attacks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Pen test vs Red Teaming
Penetration Testing
Scope-based technical assessment
  • Often white-box or grey-box with specific targets and timeboxed tests.
  • Focuses on vulnerabilities, exploitability, and remediation steps.
  • Tools: scanners, exploit frameworks; reports list findings with severity.
Example
Scan a web app, exploit SQL injection, and provide a patch recommendation.
Red Teaming
Goal-oriented adversary emulation
  • Black-box style operations that simulate real adversaries with objectives.
  • Chains multiple TTPs: social engineering, lateral movement, persistence, exfiltration.
  • Measures defender detection, response, and containment, not just vulnerabilities.
Example
Spearphish to gain credentials, move laterally to a data store, and exfiltrate files—reporting on what was detected and how quickly.
Common Mistake
Running noisy scans in a red team reduces realism and undermines measurement of detection capability.
Pro Tip
Define high-level objectives and rules of engagement early to align red and blue expectations.
Key Takeaway
Shift reports from vulnerability lists to resilience metrics tied to adversary objectives.

screens.title: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
screens.subtitle: A shared knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques

narration.text: MITRE ATT&CK is a catalog of observed attacker tactics, techniques, and common knowledge that gives red and blue teams a standard vocabulary. It maps attacker behavior across phases — from initial access to exfiltration — and assigns technique identifiers so teams can reference specific actions consistently. For red teams, ATT&CK guides scenario planning: choose techniques that match a target adversary or test a detection gap. For blue teams, ATT&CK helps map detections and controls to known techniques, revealing coverage gaps. A concrete example: initial access techniques include T1133 for External Remote Services, T1566 for Phishing, and T1078 for Valid Accounts. Using these IDs means a red team can say it simulated T1566 and the blue team can check telemetry for phishing indicators. A common misconception is that ATT&CK prescribes how to attack — it does not provide exploit code. Instead, it documents behaviours observed in the wild so teams can plan realistic emulations and measure defensive efficacy. As a takeaway, use ATT&CK as the lingua franca between offensive and defensive teams to ensure clear, actionable findings. What is MITRE ATT&CK? means att&ck is the shared taxonomy that lets teams plan emulations, map detections, and measure defensive coverage using standard ids.. In practical terms, a shared knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ATT&CK Purpose
keyIdea.text: ATT&CK is the shared taxonomy that lets teams plan emulations, map detections, and measure defensive coverage using standard IDs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › What is MITRE ATT&CK?
Core Definition
Adversary tactics, techniques, and common knowledge

ATT&CK documents observed adversary behaviour and assigns technique IDs so teams can design emulations and map detections consistently.

Plan & Scope
Select TTPs that emulate a threat group or exercise a detection gap.
Develop Scenarios
Chain techniques to reflect how adversaries operate in realistic campaigns.
Measure Defenses
Map detections to ATT&CK IDs to reveal coverage and gaps.
Quick Reference
# Example of MITRE ATT&CK TTPs for initial access:
# T1133 - External Remote Services (e.g., VPN, RDP)
# T1566 - Phishing (e.g., Spearphishing Attachment, Spearphishing Link)
# T1078 - Valid Accounts (e.g., compromised credentials)
Key Takeaway

Use ATT&CK IDs to plan realistic emulations and to map visibility gaps for defenders.

screens.title: Mapping TTPs: A Short Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Translate an attack flow into ATT&CK technique IDs

narration.text: Mapping an attack to ATT&CK is a practical skill you will use repeatedly. Start by breaking the attack into clear steps — initial access, execution, discovery, collection, and exfiltration — then assign the most relevant tactic and technique IDs. For example, if an attacker uses external credentials to enter a workstation, map that to T1078 Valid Accounts under the Initial Access tactic. If they run a PowerShell script, map execution to a command and scripting interpreter technique such as T1059. Discovery steps like enumerating network shares map to discovery techniques. The chapter provides a short snippet listing common IDs for initial access and privilege escalation; present these IDs to the blue team alongside time stamps and telemetry so defenders can tune detections. Below is the example block from the chapter rendered as a code panel: it shows T1133, T1566, T1078 for initial access and T1068, T1055, T1548 for escalation. A misconception to guard against is mapping too many techniques; choose the technique that best matches observed behaviour. Your takeaway: a focused mapping is more actionable than an exhaustive catalogue. After you map, ask: which telemetry sources would show this technique in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Mapping Practice
keyIdea.text: Break an attack into steps and assign the most representative ATT&CK IDs; present mappings with telemetry references for defenders.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Mapping TTPs: A Short Walkthrough
Process
Stepwise mapping
  1. Decompose the operation into clear phases and actions.
  2. Select the ATT&CK technique that best matches observable behaviour.
  3. Record timestamps, evidence, and telemetry sources for each mapped technique.
  4. Share mappings with blue team to tune detections and playbooks.
Common Mistake
Over-mapping to multiple techniques creates noise; prefer the best-fit technique and note alternatives.
Reference Code Block
# Example of MITRE ATT&CK TTPs for initial access:
# T1133 - External Remote Services (e.g., VPN, RDP)
# T1566 - Phishing (e.g., Spearphishing Attachment, Spearphishing Link)
# T1078 - Valid Accounts (e.g., compromised credentials)

# Example of MITRE ATT&CK TTPs for privilege escalation:
# T1068 - Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
# T1055 - Process Injection
# T1548 - Abuse of Elevated Privileges
Key Takeaway

Present concise mappings with telemetry links so defenders can validate and tune detections quickly.

screens.title: Command and Control (C2) Frameworks
screens.subtitle: Tools and infrastructure that enable persistent control during emulation

narration.text: Command and Control frameworks provide the channels and agents that allow a red team to manage compromised systems in a way that mimics real adversaries. They offer beacons or agents, communication protocols, tasking, and data exfiltration capabilities. Popular frameworks mentioned in the chapter are Cobalt Strike — a commercial tool with features such as Malleable C2 profiles and Beacon payloads — Empire (open-source PowerShell agent and Python C2 server), and Metasploit with its Meterpreter payload. When choosing a framework, red teams weigh realism, OPSEC, and the available post-exploitation features. For instance, Malleable C2 lets teams shape network indicators to mimic legitimate applications and make detection harder. A common misconception is that using powerful tooling equals better testing; instead, the right tool is the one that lets you emulate the chosen techniques while preserving OPSEC and avoiding contamination of production telemetry. In practice, document why a framework was chosen and which telemetry sources were expected to show its activity. This helps blue teams hunt and verify whether the emulation behaved like the intended adversary. Consider: when would you pick an open-source framework over a commercial one for an engagement?

keyIdea.title: C2 Selection
keyIdea.text: Choose C2 tooling that balances realism, OPSEC, and the required post-exploitation capabilities for the emulation scenario.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Command and Control (C2) Frameworks
Architecture Overview
C2 Components
  • Agents/Beacons on compromised hosts that check in and execute tasks.
  • Server-side infrastructure that issues commands, stores exfiltrated data, and manages sessions.
  • Malleable traffic profiles and transport mechanisms to blend with legitimate traffic.
Cobalt Strike
Commercial C2 with Beacon and Malleable profiles for traffic shaping.
Empire
Open-source PowerShell agent and Python C2 server for post-exploitation tasks.
Metasploit
Exploit framework with Meterpreter offering robust post-exploitation control.
Choice Criteria
Balance features, OPSEC, telemetry expectations, and the rules of engagement when selecting a framework.
Common Mistake

Picking the most feature-rich tool without planning OPSEC can create detectable artifacts and reduce the realism of the emulation.

screens.title: Malleable C2: Conceptual Profile Example
screens.subtitle: How traffic shaping makes C2 look legitimate

narration.text: Malleable C2 profiles let a red team alter network indicators so beacon traffic resembles legitimate applications. This is vital for OPSEC because it reduces the chance of simple signature-based detections. The chapter provides a simplified conceptual profile that sets an HTTP GET URI, a user agent string, several headers, and an output transformation such as base64 plus a harmless JavaScript comment. The key teaching points are not the exact text but the technique: shape headers, mimic common sites, and obfuscate payloads without leaving obvious artifacts. For example, using a user agent string matching Chrome and requesting a path like /jquery-3.5.1. min. js makes beacon traffic appear like normal web requests. A misconception is believing that changing headers alone guarantees stealth; defenders with behavioral detections or endpoint telemetry can still spot unusual sequences or timing. Your practical task is to document which telemetry — web proxies, DNS logs, and host process monitoring — you expect to reveal a malleable C2, and to include those sources when reporting. Ask yourself: which detection sources are authoritative in your environment? Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Malleable C2: Conceptual Profile
Conceptual Profile
http-get {
    set uri "/jquery-3.5.1.min.js";
    set useragent "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/100.0.4896.88 Safari/537.36";
    set header "Accept" "*/*";
    set header "Accept-Encoding" "gzip, deflate, br";
    output { base64; prepend "/* jQuery v3.5.1 | (c) JS Foundation | jquery.org/license */"; header "Content-Type" "application/javascript"; }
}
This snippet demonstrates shaping the request and obfuscating output. Remember: it is conceptual and used to illustrate OPSEC trade-offs.
Telemetry Mapping
  • Proxy and firewall logs: detect unusual host-to-domain patterns or uncommon timing.
  • DNS logs: reveal suspicious domain registrations or rapid lookups.
  • Endpoint monitoring: identify unexpected child processes or in-memory payloads.
Key Takeaway

Malleable profiles hide simple signatures; pair them with expected telemetry sources for defenders to validate and tune detections.

screens.title: Operational Security (OPSEC) for Red Teams
screens.subtitle: Protecting the realism of an engagement while avoiding collateral impact

narration.text: OPSEC keeps a red-team engagement realistic and safe. It prevents test traffic and infrastructure from contaminating production telemetry or exposing the red team. Key OPSEC practices include using dedicated infrastructure — separate C2 servers, phishing domains, and virtual machines — so that test artifacts do not appear in normal enterprise records. Red teams tailor C2 traffic to mimic legitimate flows and avoid known malicious indicators like shared public IPs flagged by threat intelligence. They prefer stealthy techniques over noisy scans and carefully plan payload deployment methods such as fileless execution or reflective DLL injection to minimize disk artifacts. However, a common misconception is that OPSEC means hiding everything; in reality, you must balance stealth with transparency defined in the rules of engagement so the blue team can safely respond without disrupting operations. Always record which telemetry sources you expect to show activity and brief incident response teams on safe containment options. The practical question to end with is: how will your OPSEC choices affect your ability to demonstrate detection gaps without unintended side effects? Operational Security (OPSEC) for Red Teams means use dedicated infrastructure, mimic legitimate traffic, avoid noisy tooling, and plan payload delivery to protect realism and safety during an engagement.. In practical terms, protecting the realism of an engagement while avoiding collateral impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OPSEC Principles
keyIdea.text: Use dedicated infrastructure, mimic legitimate traffic, avoid noisy tooling, and plan payload delivery to protect realism and safety during an engagement.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Operational Security (OPSEC)
OPSEC Checklist
Core measures to protect an engagement and maintain realism.
  • Use dedicated C2 servers, domains, and VMs separate from client infrastructure.
  • Mimic legitimate traffic using Malleable C2 rather than raw, anomalous patterns.
  • Avoid noisy scanning; choose stealthier discovery methods when possible.
  • Prefer in-memory or reflective techniques to reduce disk forensic artefacts.
Operational Notes
Coordinate with blue-team leads on response thresholds and safe containment steps to prevent accidental operational disruption.
Pitfall
Excessive secrecy that prevents the blue team from safely handling incidents can cause business impact; define transparency boundaries in advance.
Key Takeaway

OPSEC is a balance: protect realism while giving enough context and safe handling guidance to defenders.

screens.title: Designing a Red Team Engagement
screens.subtitle: From objective definition to purple-team debrief

narration.text: Designing a red team engagement begins with clear, measurable objectives. These objectives are high-level outcomes like "gain domain administrator privileges" or "exfiltrate customer data." Once objectives are agreed, select ATT&CK techniques to emulate and decide on acceptable scopes and OPSEC boundaries. Next, build or select appropriate C2 infrastructure and payloads, balancing stealth and capability. During execution, record timestamps, evidence, and telemetry sources per mapped technique so the blue team can validate detections. After the operation, hold a purple-team debrief where red and blue teams walk through the attack path, map each step to ATT&CK IDs, and identify where detections succeeded or failed. The debrief should produce actionable items: detection rules, telemetry collection changes, and playbook updates. A common mistake is omitting the telemetry mapping in reports; without it, defenders cannot reproduce or tune detections effectively. As a practical reminder, always tie findings back to the original objective: did the adversary achieve the goal, and what prevented or allowed it? That question focuses the remediation work. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Red Team Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: What to avoid to keep exercises realistic and valuable

narration.text: Even experienced teams can fall into traps that reduce the value of a red team exercise. One frequent mistake is being too noisy: aggressive scanning and obvious payloads trigger alerts and prevent a realistic assessment of stealthy adversaries. Another is failing to plan OPSEC and thereby contaminating production telemetry with test artifacts, which can mislead future incident investigations. A third pitfall is poor telemetry mapping — delivering findings without specifying which logs or events would show an attacker’s actions. That leaves defenders guessing where to look and slows remediation. Additionally, red teams sometimes misuse tools without documenting why they were chosen; defenders then cannot reproduce or validate detections. To avoid these issues, define rules of engagement that specify acceptable techniques, OPSEC constraints, and expected telemetry. Always include a mapping table that ties each attack step to ATT&CK IDs and to the telemetry sources the blue team should examine. A practical question for you: if a red team had only endpoint telemetry available, how would you select techniques to ensure the blue team can validate detections? This encourages thoughtful planning that aligns tools and observable data.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Avoid noisy tactics, OPSEC lapses, and missing telemetry mappings; plan engagements so defenders can validate and improve detections.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Common Mistakes & Misconceptions
Noisy Techniques
Aggressive scanning and loud payloads make the test unrealistic for stealthy threats.
OPSEC Lapses
Using non-dedicated infrastructure or known-malicious IPs contaminates telemetry and endangers investigations.
Missing Telemetry Mapping
Providing findings without referencing which logs or events to check leaves defenders unable to reproduce or tune rules.
Mitigation
Agree on ROEs, OPSEC boundaries, and expected telemetry sources before execution.
Reflection
Plan techniques to fit observable telemetry so blue teams can validate detections effectively.

screens.title: Purple Teaming: Turning Findings into Defense
screens.subtitle: A collaborative cycle to improve detection and response

narration.text: Purple teaming bridges offensive findings and defensive action by creating a feedback loop between red and blue teams. After an emulation, red teams should share attack chains mapped to ATT&CK IDs along with timestamps and the telemetry they expected. During the purple-team session, blue teams demonstrate what detections fired, which telemetry captured activity, and where gaps existed. The collaborative work yields concrete outputs: detection rules tied to ATT&CK techniques, instrumentation tasks to add telemetry, and incident response playbook updates. This collaborative environment reduces friction: instead of a one-way report, teams iterate on detections, run retests, and measure improvement. A key misconception is that purple teaming means the red team loses independence; in fact, controlled collaboration accelerates learning while preserving adversary realism in subsequent tests. The practical outcome should be measurable: list of detections implemented, telemetry added, and percent improvement in coverage for the emulated techniques. Ask yourself: what detection would you implement first for the mapped insider-exfiltration scenario, and why? Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Purple Teaming
Cycle
Share, Validate, Improve
  1. Red team shares mapped ATT&CK steps with evidence and expected telemetry.
  2. Blue team demonstrates which detections fired and which telemetry captured the activity.
  3. Teams agree on detection rules, telemetry to add, and playbook updates; then retest.
Deliverables

  • Telemetry enhancement list and instrumentation tasks.
  • Updated incident response playbooks with validated steps.
Key Takeaway

Make purple-team outputs specific, measurable, and tied to ATT&CK techniques so improvements are trackable.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Map an Insider Exfiltration
screens.subtitle: Practice mapping Alice's steps to ATT&CK techniques and propose detections

narration.text: Now apply what you learned to a concrete scenario: Alice, a disgruntled insider, uses her legitimate credentials to exfiltrate customer data. Break the scenario into steps: initial access via valid credentials, execution with PowerShell, discovery of network shares, collection to local storage, and exfiltration via a web upload. For each step, identify the ATT&CK tactic and the best-fit technique, for example T1078 Valid Accounts for initial access and a command-and-scripting interpreter technique for PowerShell execution such as T1059. For discovery, choose the technique that describes file and network enumeration, and for exfiltration map to a web upload exfiltration technique. After mapping, propose one concrete detection for each step and specify which telemetry you would use — host process monitoring for PowerShell, file system access logs for collection, and proxy logs for cloud uploads. A frequent mistake is listing many potential techniques without choosing the most representative one; prefer one or two targeted mappings and document alternatives. The goal of this exercise is to leave with a repeatable template: step, ATT&CK ID, telemetry sources, and one detection to implement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Detection Suggestions
  • Initial Access: monitor unusual logins and geolocation anomalies; telemetry: authentication logs.
  • Execution: detect PowerShell parent-child process relationships and encoded commands; telemetry: process monitoring and command-line auditing.
  • Discovery/Collection: alert on bulk file reads from sensitive shares; telemetry: file access logs and share enumeration history.
  • Exfiltration: flag large or unusual uploads to personal cloud domains; telemetry: proxy and DNS logs.
Key Takeaway

A mapping table with step, ATT&CK ID, telemetry, and one detection is the most actionable deliverable for defenders.

narration.text: Keep these three short reminders at hand. First, always define clear objectives for red-team work so the exercise measures resilience, not just vulnerabilities. Second, map every emulation step to ATT&CK IDs and the telemetry sources you expect to validate activity — that makes findings actionable for defenders. Third, practise OPSEC: use dedicated infrastructure and traffic shaping so tests do not contaminate production or make future detections harder to interpret.
